## Introduction & background

An H-bridge allows an MCU to drive a DC motor forwards, backwards, coast it, or brake it. It uses four solid-state switches arranged in an 'H' configuration around the motor. Turning on a diagonal pair sends current in one direction; turning on the opposite diagonal reverses it. Turning on both bottom switches shorts the motor terminals together, dissipating the motor's kinetic energy (Back-EMF) through the motor's own windings, acting as an electrical brake. The deadliest design flaw in an H-bridge is "shoot-through"—turning on both the top and bottom switches on the same side, creating a direct short circuit from the supply to ground.

## Core equations

Back-EMF (acting as a generator during braking):
$$E = K_e \cdot \omega$$

## What you're building

1. A physical motor control circuit using the DRV8833 module wired to an MCU.
2. Firmware to command four discrete operational states: forward, reverse, coast (Hi-Z), and brake.
3. A tactile physical test spinning the motor shaft by hand during both coast and brake modes to feel the mechanical resistance.
4. A hand-sketched 4-switch schematic drawn completely from memory.

## Activity

DRV8833 + small motor + MCU PWM. Implement all four states: forward, reverse, coast (both outputs Hi-Z/low), brake (both low-side on). Spin the shaft by hand in coast vs brake and feel the difference. Draw the 4-switch H-bridge from memory and mark which simultaneous pair = shoot-through.

## Question to answer

1. Why is a high-side N-FET awkward to drive (its gate must go *above* the supply when the source flies up to Vin) — and how does a bootstrap capacitor physically manufacture that higher voltage?
2. Why does dynamic braking work, and where exactly does the motor's kinetic energy go?
